Academic Ascent: Playable filler, and Draftsim's 1.0 is too harsh. A two-mana trick that also grants evasion wins combat and races in a format whose stalls break on fliers, and Empower Jace 2 is a free rider that flips your duals untapped. Last few slots in W/U or any Jace build.
Blossom-Blessed Angel // Seed Suture: Top-tier G/W common and the 1.5 grade is badly wrong. A 2/4 flier with vigilance for four both blocks the fliers that break this format's stalls and attacks into them, and the free counter-plus-life rider costs you nothing. Take it over most green commons.
Campus Crier: Filler. A 3/1 for two trades down against almost everything and dies to any ping, but it pressures early and the graveyard ability turns a dead draw into a late mana sink that untaps your duals. Last playable in W aggro, never a pick you're happy about.
Enlightened Confidant: Solid playable that becomes a real engine in G/W or W/B. Lifelink on a 2/1 means you usually gain exactly 2, so it rebuys one- and two-drops — fine, not free. A 2/1 body dies to every common trick or ping, so it needs a board already ahead.
Fateshaper Aspirant: Solid playable, and the 1.5 grade is too harsh. Echoed pairs mean 'legendary card in your graveyard' is almost always live, so this is a body plus a card back; the counter-plus-indestructible mode blows out a block or a removal spell. Five mana is the only real knock.
Flickering Hound: Filler dressed as a rare. Four mana for a 2/2 is below the format's rate, and the blink only pays when you have real ETB creatures plus a creature-heavy curve to trigger it. The removal-dodge blink is cute but reactive. Play it in a W deck stacked with enter-the-battlefield value, cut it otherwise.
Generous Revival: Low-end playable, not the 1.0 Draftsim has it at. Two bodies across a long game is real in a grindy format, but it needs a worthwhile three-drop already dead and the flashback costs five. Fine 22nd card in W/B attrition, cut from anything proactive.
Germinate Recruits: Trap. Three mana that does literally nothing unless you already gained life this turn, and even in G/W Vigorbloom you need a lifelink connection plus this in hand simultaneously. A rare you should not maindeck; the 0.5 is earned.
Graft Surgeon: Playable filler that Draftsim underrates. A 3/3 for three is on rate in a format where three damage kills most things, and the counter surviving its death means it never trades down. Best in R/W and G/W where counters have other homes.
Guiding Hydra: Bomb in any deck with bodies, and the X makes it castable on turn three or turn eight. The counters it hands out are permanent, so even after it's killed you keep the board growth — first-pick material in R/W Ajani's Army and G/W Vigorbloom. Dead on an empty board.
Hexhaven Battalion: Solid top-end common: six power across three bodies plus a Jace, and the landcycling floor means it is never a dead card in a clunky opener. Best in R/W and W/B where Cadet count feeds Kindred Judgment and Command the Stage; take it over filler, not over removal.
Kindred Judgment: Slow but genuinely one-sided — name Soldier and your Cadets walk away from a full wrath. Seven mana in a normal-speed format means you need a defensive deck that actually reaches turn seven, so it's a high pick for W/x control and a mediocre one in R/W go-wide.
Loyal Tutor: Unplayable. Jace tokens are tokens, not planeswalker cards, so this tutors nothing unless you opened an actual planeswalker — and even then you pay a card and a mana to draw it a turn later. Leave it in the box.
Memory Trap: Premium white removal at common — unconditional exile of any nonland permanent, answering bombs, equipment and the Jace token alike. Sorcery speed and the risk of a blowout if it's removed keep it a notch behind Prophesied End, but it's an early pick in any white deck.
Predictive Preparations: Filler that wants a wide board. Sorcery-speed pump is the weakest interaction rate in the set, but splitting two counters across two bodies plus flashback makes it a slow two-for-one. Only in R/W counters or G/W, and only after your creature count is real.
Prophesied End: Premium removal and the best rate in the set's common slot — two mana, instant, kills anything, and the card they draw is refundable by just waiting for them to attack. The 2.5 grade is too low; take this over almost any two-drop creature.
Refute Destiny: Sideboard all-star, maindeck liability. The rate is premium — two-mana unconditional exile with upside — but it only answers green or blue, and G/U is the pair fewest drafters end up in. Take it, board it in against the two colors it hits, cut it otherwise.
Repurposed Enforcer: Solid early playable. A 3/2 for two attacks well in a format where three damage kills most things, and the empower rider is stapled profit on a card you'd already run — it turns your duals untapped and fuels the Jace draw engine. Best in go-wide R/W and W/U aggro, fine anywhere white.
Shatterwing Pegasus: Graded far too low at 1.5 — this is a solid common. A three-mana 2/3 flier dodges the format's 3-damage removal on defense, blocks the W/U fliers, and closes stalled boards, which is exactly how games end here. The pump is late-game rider, not the reason.
Surgical Precision: Better than its grade. Toughness 4+ covers about a third of the format's creatures — exactly the ones white can't fight through — and the second mode means it never rots in hand. A two-mana removal-or-cantrip that always does something is a solid main-deck common.
Unflinching Hortimancer: Fine aggressive two-drop, meaningfully better in G/W. Ward {1} on a cheap body taxes the removal-dense black and red decks, and any lifegain density turns it into a threat that must be answered on curve. In a deck with no lifegain it's just a 2/1.
Your Fate Ends Here: Premium white removal and I'd take it over the Draftsim grade suggests. Unconditional destroy at instant speed with a free surveil; the mana-value-3 floor only misses one- and two-drops, and this format's stalls are broken by expensive things anyway. Second-best white answer after Prophesied End.
Countersculpt: Filler. Two mana is only the real cost once a Jace token is already out, and holding up counterspells in a grindy creature format loses tempo you rarely get back. Playable in a W/U or G/U deck light on interaction, otherwise a sideboard card.
Cruel Calculations: Trap at three mana. Nothing in the card mills, so it only draws more than one when you've already surveiled or cast a mill spell that same turn — realistically a sorcery-speed Divination in U/B and a blank anywhere else. Well below the grade; treat it as a 23rd card.
Cryotheory Adept: Solid U/R two-drop, better than the 1.5 suggests. One toughness is a real liability when three damage is everywhere, but prowess makes it trade up early and the graveyard activation turns a dead late draw into a two-turn tap-down. Filler outside Chandra's Prowess.
Diviner of Victory // Unwind History: Role-player, not a rare you move into. The free bounce is real tempo in W/U surveil aggro and the body grows on every scry or surveil trigger, but a 1/1 for one is a bad topdeck and the spell caps at mana value three. Fine playable, mid-pack pick.
Divining Duelist: Solid playable, and I'd grade it above Draftsim's read. Flash 3/2 for three ambushes most of the format's two- and three-drops, and the tap mode either pushes a lethal attack or blanks a blocker for a turn. Loot mode gives it a floor when the board is empty. W/U tempo wants it.
Icy Reception: Playable tempo, not an answer. Blue kills nothing, so this is the fair version: a Force Spike that hits creatures and — because echoed legends are everywhere — plenty of noncreature spells too. The -5/-0 mode is an emergency combat blank. Fine filler in W/U and U/R.
Infinite Coursework: Blue's best answer, which says more about blue than about the card. Losing all abilities and never untapping is a cleaner lock than Pacifism, and unpreparing a prepared creature steals its free spell. Still an enchantment, not an answer — it dies to bounce and eats a card. Fine W/U and U/R playable.
Jace's Machinations: Build-around, not a bomb. Eight loyalty is a lot of stored surveil-and-draw, but it affects nothing the turn you cast it and you still only get one activation per turn, so it's three mana for future card flow. Real payoff needs Compel Brutality or a Jace sacrifice outlet. Mostly a G/U trap.
Mindseeker Oculus: Mid playable whose value is entirely the empower, not the 2/1. Four loyalty in one shot turns your duals on, gives the token real draw activations, and makes Compel Brutality lethal. Good in any blue deck that wants a cheap body; don't let it pull you into the G/U trap.
Perfected Theory: Underrated at 0.5. Blue has no kill spells, so a one-mana instant that turns their bomb into a 1/1 in combat is the closest thing W/U or U/R gets to an answer, and the 4/5 mode steals races. Needs a blocker; still playable filler.
Plan for All Outcomes: Trap at four mana. It touches the board without answering anything — they choose top, so you often buy one turn — and the empower trigger only pays off in G/U, the pair with the least removal. Mark it well below the grade; this is a late pick.
Precise Redaction: Sideboard card, not a maindeck spell. Two-mana hard counter is a premium rate, but blind against R/G or U/x it's a blank in a colour that already can't kill anything. Board it in against W/B attrition and it's one of the best cards in your 40.
Protege's Awakening: Trap for G/U drafters. Four mana that affects nothing on board, replaces itself and leaves a Jace that needs several turns of −3s to actually profit. The huge empower number is cosmetic since every empower feeds the same token; last-slot playable only.
Semester Foreseer // Peer Review: Much better than its grade. Four mana for a 3/4 that dodges the format's 3-damage removal, then a free 2/2 Cadet and two surveil triggers off one card — that's two bodies and deck sculpting in the W/U surveil deck. Solidly maindeckable common, take it over most filler.
Sphinx of False Conclusions: First-pickable and blue's best threat. Four power in the air on a flash body closes games fast, and the death-copy means their removal buys a turn, not an answer — they have to kill it twice while you loot toward your best cards. Two toughness is the only knock.
Sphinx's Approach: The tutor half is fiction in Limited — you will never own five copies — so evaluate it as an instant-speed draw two for three. That's honest filler in the grindy U/B and U/W decks and better than the 1.0 grade implies, but it never affects the board.
Surveillance Phantasm: Underrated — this is a 2/3 flier with vigilance for two in the deck that's already surveilling, and the {3}{U} ability means it turns itself on with no help. Surveil is the set's most-used keyword and the Jace token does it for free. Real W/U playable, not a wall.
The Theorist, Jace Beleren: Bomb, first pick out of any pack. Four mana for an extra card every turn cycle that also defends itself with chump blockers and bounces the thing attacking it. You win the long game from the turn it resolves, and the format goes long.
Theorist's Proxy: Role-player dressed as a rare. A two-mana 0/3 flash blocker that hands you an immediate 3-loyalty Jace is real — one activation from drawing a card, and it turns your duals untapped — but nothing here pressures anyone. Uncounterable is blank in Limited. Fine in G/U, skippable elsewhere.
Undulating Witness: Better than its grade — a genuine blue common you're happy to run. A 3/5 flier dodges the format's three-damage removal, blocks the ground, and closes stalled boards, and the pump turns extra mana into reach. The landcycling floor means it's never a dead card. Solid mid-pick, not a late scoop.
Unsummon: Tempo filler, never an answer — blue kills nothing, so this just resets a bomb for a turn or saves a creature from removal. Playable one-of in a curve-out W/U tempo deck, first cut for any deck planning to go long.
Variable Chaser // Arc of Fortune: Draft it for the body. A 2/3 flier with prowess for three is a fine W/U or U/R clock; the free wheel refuels your opponent just as hard and is only correct when you're hellbent and they aren't. Good card, bad button.
Apex Witchstalker: Solid top-end common and a bad 1.5. Six mana 6/4 menace closes games that stall, the drain gives it value even when it trades, and basic landcycling means it is never a dead card in your opener. Play one, cycle the second.
Bloodline Recollector // Ancestral Cravi: Play it as a two-drop and treat the back half as a lottery ticket. Black is the thinnest colour at two mana, so a 2/2 body earns the slot on its own; three creatures dying in one turn realistically only happens in W/B attrition with a sacrifice outlet. Filler, not a mythic.
Break Under Pressure: Better than its grade — instant-speed answer to the opponent's best creature that ignores hexproof, indestructible and untargetability, with two life on top. It whiffs against a wide board where the biggest thing is a token, so pair it with real removal rather than leaning on it.
Cast Away Doubt: Playable, not the near-blank the grade implies. Three mana for two cards is a real rate in a format that goes long, and the two damage is upside rather than cost in B/R, where noncombat damage to the opponent turns on the whole reach package. Cut it from any deck that's racing.
Dark Matter Manipulator: Strong U/B enabler, not a standalone rare. A one-mana body that self-mills three is exactly the on-ramp to threshold, and it scales to a 3/2 then 5/2 as the yard fills. In any deck that isn't digging for seven cards, it's a 1/2 you cut.
Extended Absence: Top black common and the 2.0 grade undersells it badly. Unconditional instant-speed exile that also hits planeswalkers, with a two-point life swing attached; four mana is the only cost. Speed matters less in a format this grindy — pick it over most creatures.
Extrapolate the Impossible: Unplayable. Cards from outside the game don't exist in a draft or prerelease pool, so this is a blank you can't cast for value. Never maindeck it, never sideboard it. The zero grade is correct.
Last Gasp: Premium common. Two-mana instant -3/-3 covers 68% of the set's creatures and kills two-for-one ETB bodies on the stack of combat. Black's workhorse alongside No Admittance — take it over any common creature and most uncommons.
Lich's Relic: First-pickable. Pay three mana total and unconditionally destroy any creature or planeswalker, then keep a +2/+1 Equipment on the battlefield — removal that doesn't fully trade a card. Cheaper and more flexible than Extended Absence. The 3.5 grade undersells it; this is close to a black bomb.
Multiply by Zero: Premium removal and one of black's best uncommons. Two mana at instant speed kills anything regardless of size — no toughness cap like Last Gasp, no mana-value clause — and it answers bombs the rest of the set can't. Only +1/+1 counters and anthems beat it. Take it over most creatures.
Overwrite the Multiverse: First-pick bomb. A six-mana exile-everything wipe in a creature format wins games on its own, and the empower leaves you a loaded Jace to grind out the rebuild while your opponent starts over. Only build caveat: you want the controlling half of your pair, not the aggro half.
Rampart Hunter: Graded far too low. Four-mana 3/3 deathtouch already brick-walls the format's top end, and the ETB is a free trick — pump a blocker into a removal spell or swing as a 5/5 deathtouch. Real B/G and W/B playable, mid-pack common.
Rank Rat: Marginal but real, because black is the shallowest colour at two drops. The discard only bites on turn two and fades to nothing later, so you're paying for a 1/1 body. Fine in W/B where the body dies for value; cut it from slower decks.
Rewrite Regrets: Late-round value, not a playable you're excited about. Four mana to rebuy your best dead creature is fine in a grindy U/B or W/B deck, but it's a blank in your opening hand and needs the game to have already gone badly. The empower rider doesn't change the pick.
Rise of the Deathbringer: Strong rare, and the sweeper mode is the point: −3/−3 at instant speed kills most of the format and you choose to fire it after blocks. Mode two refills when the board is already yours. Wants a B/x deck that can build around going bigger or wider.
Sanctum Lurker: Grade this up. It makes its own Jace token, keeps it alive at zero loyalty, and turns it into a repeatable drain-1 — a three-mana 3/2 that also wins long games by itself, which is exactly the 'is one 2-loyalty token enough' test most planeswalker payoffs fail. Strong in B/x attrition.
Screeching Soulbreaker: Undervalued at 1.5 — this is a real B/R common. Toughness four walls the format's three-damage ground creatures, and it attacks past them for a drain every turn. The chip damage also switches on Massacre Girl's counters and recurs Command the Stage.
Silence the Echo: Playable removal with a tax, not premium. At {1}{B} plus a sacrifice it's only clean when you have a spent Jace token or an already-fired prepared body; otherwise it's a four-mana sorcery to kill one thing. Good in W/B attrition, mediocre elsewhere.
Solve for Disappointment: Near-filler. Sorcery-speed discard is card-neutral at best, gives up tempo, and is the worst topdeck in a format where games go long. The empower rider is a real but small consolation — one loyalty doesn't buy a card. Twenty-third card in a black deck.
Terminal Criticism: Premium rate, punishing condition. Against U/R or any blue-red deck this is a two-mana unconditional kill that also answers planeswalkers; against B/G or R/W it is a blank. Sideboard all-star, and a maindeck card only when your removal count is thin.
Theoretical Necromancer: Fine aggressive common. Four power for three pressures immediately and trades up, but one toughness means every ping and every block kills it. The real value is the graveyard activation late, which also feeds U/B threshold. Middle-of-the-pack for B/R and W/B, never an early pick.
Void Extrapolator // Omit Variables: Good common for U/B, filler elsewhere. Black is thin on two-drops, so a 2/2 that arrives with a free mill three matters, and threshold at seven is realistic in a deck built for it — the +1/+1 keeps it relevant late. In any other pair the mill is worse than blank.
Vraska's Final Mercy: Premium removal and the best rate in the set — two mana, unconditional, hits planeswalkers, and the two life is nothing outside a race. Draftsim's 3.0 undersells it badly; this is a top-two pick out of the pack and pulls you into black. The empower mode is a rider you'll rarely take.
Ajani's Anguish: Scalable removal that leaves an anthem behind. Sorcery speed and X=3 costing four mana makes it clunky against the removal benchmarks, but it goes face and the trample matters in R/G once you have Heartwood fatties. Playable, not a first pick.
Artifist Acumen: Filler, and only in U/R. Sorcery speed kills it as a trick — you can't ambush a blocker — so this is a one-mana cantrip that occasionally steals a race with first strike. Take it as a prowess enabler, never as interaction.
Awaken the Inferno: Solid red common purely because it never rots in your hand — landcycling for {2} is the floor, six damage killing literally anything is the ceiling. Five mana is well off red's efficient rates, so it's your third or fourth removal spell, not the one you take over a two-drop.
Blazing Crescendo: Filler trick that mostly pays for itself. +3/+1 wins combat against the toughness-3 middle of the format and the impulse card keeps it from being a blowout when they have the answer. Real value only as a cheap noncreature spell in U/R prowess or R/W.
Chandra's Emberling: Filler, and only in U/R. A three-mana 2/2 haste is under rate, and it needs a genuinely spell-dense deck to grow before it eats a removal spell or a trade. Fine as a 22nd card if you're already the prowess deck; unplayable outside it.
Command the Stage: Deck-dependent engine. In B/R, where noncombat damage is the whole plan, it recurs every upkeep and the format's long games turn that into an unanswerable stream of bodies; in R/W it grows the Cadet board instead. Anywhere else it's a three-mana 2/2 sorcery — unplayable.
Craterclaw Colossus: Bomb in R/G Heartwood ramp, overrated at 5.0 anywhere else. Seven mana with triple red buys a 5/5 haste and an alpha strike that usually ends the game — but only if you've built the artifact count and the ramp to cast it on time. Do not first-pick it into an unknown lane.
Curse-Marred Demon: First-pickable red rare. A four-mana 4/4 flier with trample already outclasses the format's removal benchmarks — toughness four dodges the 3-damage commons — and the tutor turns it into your bomb plus a threat. Random discard is a rounding error when you're up two good cards.
Draconic Visitor: Bomb. Five mana for a 5/5 flier already ends games in a format where three damage is the common removal ceiling and toughness 4 dodges most of it. In R/G the replacement clause turns every Heartwood token into another 5/5 dragon — that is unbeatable.
Eardrum Rattler: Filler two-drop you play for the body. The unblockable ability is capped at power two and costs mana every turn, so it only matters in R/W go-wide or B/R when you need the last few points. A 2/2 for two is the card; the text is a bonus.
Essence Burn: Sideboard all-star, maindeck liability. Five damage with exile for two mana is a premium rate, but it only points at black and green permanents, so roughly half your game ones it's a dead card in hand. Board it in against B/x and G/x and it's near-first-pickable; never start it blind.
Face Yourself: Trap, and the 0.0 is close to right. Seven mana, does nothing unless your opponent already has a board, and the tokens evaporate at end of turn unless you control a planeswalker. A Jace token makes the copies stick permanently, which is the only reason to look twice — still unplayable in most decks.
Fulminous Forte: Premium removal, take it over most creatures. Five damage at instant speed kills essentially anything in the format, and the one-sided one-damage sweep is a blowout against W/U Cadet boards and R/W go-wide. Flexibility like this is what you want in red.
Hallway Heckler // Vicious Verse: Better than a 1.0 in B/R. A 2/3 for three blocks the format's early aggression, the free point of face damage plays into B/R's reach plan, and the rummage ability fuels U/B threshold late. Nothing special, but a fine 22nd-23rd card.
Heartstring Puller: Good aggressive common: five power across two bodies for four mana, and the 3/1 trample body wants the Cadet to clear a blocker. Best in R/W go-wide where the token also feeds Kindred Judgment and Command the Stage. The 3/1 dies to everything, so lead with it, don't hold it.
Identity Echo: Unplayable. Three mana does nothing, then four more to exile your own body for a random creature off the top — that is seven mana for a coin flip that can easily downgrade your board. Never maindeck it.
Master of Barbs: Premium two-drop in B/R and near-unplayable outside it. A 2/1 menace is an acceptable aggro body on its own, and every ping, burn spell to the face, or Stingerquill attack trigger turns it into a team anthem that pushes lethal through blockers. Draft it high once you're in the pair.
No Admittance: Premium common removal, take it early over most creatures. Three damage at instant-relevant cost kills the large majority of the set's creatures, hits face when you need the last points, and the empower rider is pure profit: untapped duals plus a Compel Brutality target later.
Pompous Battlemage // Improvised Act: Filler rare. A 1/1 prowess body for one with a free loot is playable in a dedicated U/R spells deck that wants cheap prowess bodies, and close to unplayable outside it. Late pick, not a reason to be red.
Pyre Rhymer // Molten Tide: Judge it as a three-mana 3/3 prowess and stop there. The prepared spell is a one-shot Mountain ritual, which does almost nothing in a Limited game and costs you the prepared body's flexibility. Fine U/R playable on rate alone; don't pay a premium for the split card.
Skilled Battlecarver: Solid aggressive filler for B/R and R/W. First strike on your turn means it attacks into 3/3s profitably and the firebreathing gives late-game mana somewhere to go. It blocks badly, so only play it in a deck that means to be the attacker.
Stingcaster Mage: Good, not the 4.0 the grade claims. You pay full retail for the flashback, so this is often just a two-mana 2/1 haste early, and only mid-game does it become a body plus a rebought removal spell. Real in U/R prowess and B/R; not a card that wins a game alone.
Tether Technician: Fine common filler. A 4/5 with reach at five mana blanks the fliers and Heartwood-ramped attackers that break this format's boards, and the optional discard converts a flooded land into two damage. The ETB is a bonus, not a reason. Playable in any red deck; the grade undersells the body.
Violent Echoes: Premium removal — six damage at instant speed kills literally anything in the set, and the excess turns into loyalty so overkill is upside. The double red is the only real cost. Draftsim's 3.0 is low; take this over most uncommon creatures and be happy in any red deck.
Wrath of the Bloodmane: Best red common in the set and the grade is a point low. Legends are everywhere in FRA thanks to the echoed pairs, so this is usually a two-mana instant for four damage — the step past three damage that kills the toughness-4 dodgers. First-pick common.
Arcane Amphisbaena: Good common, above the grade. A two-mana deathtouch body trades with anything the ramp decks land, and the empower is free profit — it turns your common duals on untapped and builds a Jace that Compel Brutality can point at a creature.
Bestial Incursion: Better than the grade — this is a top green common. A 4/4 trample is above the curve for four mana in a format where three damage kills most things, and flashback makes it two cards in a set that goes long. Take it early and don't cut it.
Budding Insurgent: Graded far too low. A 3/3 vigilance for three is a fine green common on rate, and the sacrifice mode answers Pacifism effects, Equipment and the legendary Ways for free upside. Maindeck it as a body and treat the naturalize as a bonus.
Carnivorous Cultivator // Enroot: A two-mana 2/3 deathtouch is a beating in a format where three damage is the standard removal size — that body alone makes it a strong playable. The prepared half only fuels threshold and its own recursion, so this is a good common wearing a rare's frame rather than a pick-one.
Compel Brutality: Green's best common answer, but discount it anyway. It's a one-sided bite rather than a fight, so you don't take damage back — still, it needs a body already down and it gets blown out by instant-speed removal in response. The loyalty mode is only live in Jace-heavy builds.
Flourishing Grapple: Sideboard all-star, maindeck liability. A one-mana fight that also strips abilities is a premium rate, but it only points at red or white permanents and you also need a body on board. Board it in against R/W; leave it out game one.
Gardenize: Trap and basically unplayable. It affects nothing the turn it lands, needs your creatures to die before it does anything, and then only makes main-phase mana in a deck that already ramps with Heartwood tokens. Three mana for a card that never blocks or attacks.
Greenhouse Propagator: Role-player that does two jobs badly and both jobs adequately. A 2/3 body blocks the format's two-drops, the mana ability ramps to your five-drops in R/G, and the lifegain trigger switches on G/W's payoffs. Playable in every green deck, exciting in none.
Heartwood Crafter // Soul Tether: Solid R/G early pick. One mana for a body plus a free Heartwood later is two cards for one, and the Heartwood ramps you a turn ahead into Konstrari's top end while counting as an artifact for Pia and friends. The restricted {C} is minor — it still activates abilities.
Hexhaven Invigorator: The grade is badly wrong — a 6/6 vigilance for four mana beats anything this format presents on curve, and it attacks without opening the door. The quadruple green is the whole cost of admission, so it's base-green only. The damage-triggered ramp is nearly irrelevant. First-pickable if you're already in green.
Hungering Puppetbeast: Near-bomb and the one green rare you happily first-pick. Five mana for a 5/5 that brings its own Heartwood is already above rate, and the sac ability gives it hexproof to blank removal or trample to end the game. R/G ramp wants it most; any green deck plays it.
Hunter's Axe: Cheap and better than it looks in a creature deck. One mana down, equip two, and deathtouch-on-attack means every swing forces a bad block; trample mode punishes chumps. Green needs this because its 'removal' is fight effects. Solid in B/G and R/G, weak in a low-body pool.
Inspired Tethermage: Playable body, ignore the payoff text. A 3/2 for three is fine on its own; the growth clause only matters if you're already deep in empower cards, and the {6} activation is a mana sink you'll rarely afford. Filler outside a committed G/U build.
Puppet Crafting: Build-around rare, unplayable outside R/G. Heartwood tokens turn it into a two-mana 5/5 that still taps for mana, and the graveyard recursion insures against the two-for-one. With no artifacts or enchantments in your pool it's a sideboard card, so don't move in on it early.
Restore with Empathy: Narrow role-player. Instant-speed regrowth on any permanent is real card advantage but does nothing early and needs something already dead. The four life makes it a live enabler in G/W Vigorbloom; elsewhere it is a 23rd card at best.
Simulacrum Shaper: Solid role-player, a touch under the grade. Three mana for a 2/2, a tapped land, and a card when it dies is fine value, but fixing is close to free here with ten common duals, so you're paying for ramp and a replaceable body. Best in R/G, where the extra land finds real top-end.
Something Worth Saving: Marginal filler that does nothing to the board. It replaces itself only if a permanent is in the top four, and the gain-one is noise. The mill matters in U/B threshold and B/G, where it's a fine 22nd card; anywhere else it's the first cut.
Sureshot Sower: Solid green common and better than a 1.5. A 3/1 reach two-drop trades up early and holds off the fliers this format uses to break stalls, then converts to a hard answer for a flier late when it's stopped attacking. Green wants exactly this shape.
Tarmogoyf: Solid green two-drop, not the mythic its name implies. By turn four it's usually a 2/3 or 3/4 for two, which beats most bodies it meets, but it has no evasion, no text and no reach — it stops mattering exactly when the format's fliers take over. Good early pick, never a bomb.
Tethermage's Advantage: Near-last pick. One mana for +2/+2 and an untap is a genuine ambush blocker and it can steal a race, but it is still card disadvantage in a format where repeatable value breaks stalls. Sideboard against fliers; cut it from most maindecks.
Verdant Kraken: Bomb, with a real cost. Seven mana and triple green keeps it out of splashes, but a 6/6 that adds a 3/3 land creature every single upkeep — including the opponent's — ends the game about two turns after it resolves. If you're green, this is your first pick.
Vinelasher Adept: Late-pick with a floor. Six mana for a 2/4 body plus three counters is clunky value that does nothing if they kill the target in response, and the reach is the best part of the statline. Landcycling means it's never dead. Twenty-third card in green; cycle it more often than you cast it.
Wrecking Gecko: Draftsim's 0.5 is simply wrong. A five-mana 5/5 common with ward 2 is a top-end body that taxes the format's cheap removal out of range — most decks need two spells or a chump block. It's clunky and the firebreathing is fake, but this is a real green common, not a sideboard card.
Aerid Konstrari: Bomb, first pick out of the pack. A four-mana 5/4 flier ends games on its own in a format where stalls break on evasion, and it pays ramp on both entry and death so removal never fully answers it. Gold cost means R/G or nothing.
Avatar of Burgeoning Echoes: Strong two-drop engine, but shackled to the format's worst pair. Every land drop is two loyalty, so Jace is drawing a card every other turn by turn five — real card advantage off a body that blocks. The ultimate is decoration. Worth first-picking only if G/U is open.
Blessed Ghoul: Filler that earns its slot in W/B and nowhere else. Hybrid means it costs one mana in either colour, and the recursion turns spare late-game mana into repeatable death triggers and lifelink chip. Fine 23rd card, never a card you prioritize.
Bloombrute: The G/W signpost and a genuine first-pick in the pair — 4/4 for four is above rate before the trigger, so the card draw is pure profit in a deck that gains life incidentally. Just remember G/W has the least removal, so do not force it from a single early pick.
Charge the Sanctum: Near the bottom of the playables. Three mana for +2/+0 is a bad rate even at instant speed, and the single-target mode leaves a permanent counter but still costs you a card. Only consider it in the widest R/W boards where the team mode is a surprise kill; otherwise sideboard.
Clash of Elements: Best answer available to a blue deck, and the U/R signpost earns the pick. Blue otherwise cannot kill anything, so a two-mode Time Ebb that either eats their draw step for two damage or buries the permanent on the bottom is as close to removal as the colour gets. Answers bombs.
Craftwork Crusher: The R/G payoff and a legitimate first pick if you're already in the pair. Four damage plus a body plus a card off one ETB is three cards of value, and a 7/5 trampler closes immediately. Seven mana with RRGG means you need Heartwood tokens to cast it on curve.
Denzilore Fatehold: Bomb and a first pick out of the pack. Flash 3/4 flier for four is already a premium ambush, and W/U is the surveil pair — 43 cards in the set trigger it and the Jace token does it for free, so every activation grows your whole board. Wins stalls by itself.
Desperate Futurescribe: Take this first out of a W/U pack. A four-mana 3/4 flier is above rate on its own and outclasses the cheap fliers the pair is built on; with surveil on 43 cards the counter mode is effectively always on, so it grows a second threat every combat.
Emergency Phytomedic // Seed Suture: Playable filler, a notch better than the 1.5 suggests. One hybrid mana gets a body now and a counter plus a life later, which is two cards' worth of tempo in G/W Vigorbloom where the counter and the lifegain both trigger something. Just a 1/1; never a high pick.
Entrust the Spark: Unplayable. In Limited you almost never have a planeswalker card in your deck to find, and sacrificing a Jace token to search for nothing is the realistic outcome. Five mana, two colors, zero board impact. Do not maindeck this even in G/U.
Fatehold Charm: Solid W/U playable — a two-mana instant that's never dead is exactly what a tempo deck wants. The bounce mode also answers a spell on the stack, and the team pump steals races out of nowhere. Not a first pick, but it makes the deck every time and rewards holding mana up.
Fatehold Chronologist // Peer Review: One of the better commons in W/U. Two mana for a flier, then a free 2/2 Cadet plus surveil later — two bodies and a trigger from one card, all on hybrid mana so it's castable in either half. Fuels Proft and the other surveil payoffs.
Ferocity of the Hunt: Much better than a 0.5. Flash deathtouch ambushes anything they attack with, and the recursion clause means you're insulated from the usual aura blowout — if they kill your creature in response you still get it back. A real trick in B/G.
Frostbite Pyromental: Fringe rare despite the stats — a three-mana hasty 4/4 trample that draws two is only that if it connects, and any 2/2 blocker reduces it to a three-mana Nothing. Playable in a low-curve U/R prowess deck racing on an empty board; cut it from anything grindier.
Grim Repriser: Above its grade. A prowess two-drop in the pair with the thinnest two-drop depth, and B/R is the archetype most likely to have chipped in noncombat damage, so the recursion is close to an every-game ability. Strong early pick in the format's best pair.
Ingris Stingerquill: First-pick quality in B/R and worth committing to. A 1/4 flier blocks everything the format's aggro decks present while every attack drains the opponent, and the Cadet-plus-haste sink converts spare mana into an immediate clock. The triple-pip cost means you're in the pair, not splashing.
Konstrari Charm: Bottom-of-the-deck R/G filler, though 1.0 is a touch low. Every mode is narrow — six damage that only hits fliers, a counters trick, two mana of ramp — but flier removal is the scarce effect in a format whose stalls break in the air. Twenty-second card, sideboard elsewhere.
Konstrari Improviser // Soul Tether: Above-rate common for R/G. A 2/2 hybrid two-drop that also hands you a Heartwood token is a body plus a ramp step for two mana, and it feeds the artifact-count payoffs. Higher than the 2.0 grade in the pair; unremarkable outside it.
Kwia Vigorbloom: Bomb, full stop. A 6/6 flying vigilance lifelink body ends the game in two swings, blocks everything, and ward {2} means their one removal spell probably doesn't answer it. The Lotus trigger is gravy you'll rarely need. Take it over anything and splash the second white if you have to.
Mind Meanderer: Strong card, weak home. Six mana buying a 4/4 flier plus a fight removes a blocker and leaves the best body on board — that is a game-winner. But it lives only in G/U, the pair with the fewest removal spells; play it if you are there, do not move in for it.
Null Summoner: Strong U/B rare. A 4/2 for four that strips their best card is already fine, and threshold at seven — exactly what Theorix is built to hit — turns the exiled card into yours, castable off any mana. Two toughness is the weakness; it dies to nearly everything in red and black.
Paradox Shaper // Omit Variables: One of the best uncommons for U/B and a real engine. The free mill three every upkeep hits threshold at seven fast and never costs a card, and the hybrid cost makes it castable in either color alone. The graveyard-to-bottom ability rebuys your best card and shuts off opposing threshold. Take it highly in U/B.
Primal Witchstalker: Good B/G signpost, mediocre in a vacuum. The 2/1 menace is small for three, so this lives on the mill four — it fuels threshold and graveyard payoffs and occasionally buys a land back. Take it high once you're in B/G, let it wheel otherwise.
Proctor of Potential: Aggressive and hard to kill permanently. A two-mana 3/1 that surveils off every creature you play, then buys itself back from the yard for two, is exactly the W/U Fatehold plan. The 3/1 body trades down, but the recursion turns each trade into profit.
Prudent Fateseer // Peer Review: Good W/U uncommon. Three mana buys a 1/4 wall that stonewalls the aggro starts plus a free 2/2 and a surveil later, and the once-a-turn team pump converts W/U's surveil density into unexpected damage. Two bodies on one card is where the value is.
Recursive Recruitment: Strong U/B uncommon and an early pick in the pair. Four mana for two 2/2s is a fair rate that trades up and blocks fliers-adjacent ground stalls, then the flashback is a real late-game mana sink that scales with the graveyard you're filling anyway. Two cards from one slot.
Solarium Sentry: Rate beats text: a 3/3 for two is an aggressive body any G/W or white deck wants, and the opponent's cheap spells will trigger lifegain often enough to feed Bloombrute and the Vigorbloom payoffs. Grade it as a playable two-drop, not as a build-around rare.
Solitary Cell: Efficient, conditional removal. Two mana to exile anything with mana value three or less catches most of the format, but it whiffs entirely on the top end and gives the permanent back if the artifact is destroyed. The legendary-discard loot is live constantly given how many legends this set prints. Good R/W playable, not a bomb.
Stingerquill Charm: Premium removal in the best pair. Two mana, instant speed, three damage anywhere is already a top common rate, and the first-strike-deathtouch and hasty Cadet modes mean it's never stranded. Take it over almost any B/R creature.
Stingerquill Voxmancer // Vicious Verse: An engine with a tiny payload — judge it by the deck. In B/R face burn, a one-mana body that fires a free ping at their head every upkeep is a real clock and turns on the noncombat-damage payoffs. In any other deck it's a 1/2 that does nothing.
Stinging Vitriol: Narrow — good in B/R Stingerquill, mediocre everywhere else. Two mana for two face damage and their best nonland card does nothing to the board, so it's only worth it when noncombat damage is a payoff you're building around. In any other black-red pool this trades your card for their worst.
Tam's Resistance: Marginal, G/U only. Sorcery-speed single counter is not a card, so you are paying two mana to make a Jace token that draws you one card and turns your duals untapped. That is real value, just slow value. Last few slots if you are already in the Jace deck.
Tenured Tethermage: Good engine, slightly over-graded at 4.0. Trading a land for two Heartwoods is net ramp plus two artifacts, and tapping them for two counters each turn makes this a growing threat. The tension is real — mana or counters, not both — and a 1/1 body dies before you get either. R/G only.
Theorix Charm: Solid U/B playable, not premium. Two mana at instant speed that's always live is worth real slots — but -2/-2 misses a good chunk of the format's bodies and the soft counter is a tax, not an answer. The mill-and-draw mode fuels threshold when nothing else applies. Good twenty-third card, not an early pick.
Theorix Metamage // Omit Variables: Better than the 1.5 suggests. A three-mana 2/3 that becomes a 3/3 flier is a fine common body, and the free mill three both digs toward that threshold and feeds the U/B graveyard plan. Solid maindeck common in U/B; a plain 2/3 elsewhere.
Twinned Vision: Filler that counts as a spell. Cantrip now, then three mana to loot-and-draw-two later, which is fine in U/R Chandra's Prowess where the spell count itself is a payoff. In any other deck it's a card that doesn't affect the board. Last playables.
Twisted Fates: Solid W/B anchor, not premium removal. Five mana at WWB is a real cost and sorcery speed is a downgrade from the format's best answers, but hitting any nonland permanent plus a one-sided anthem wins the board on the spot. First-pickable in the pair, not out of it.
Uldaros Theorix: First-pick bomb. A six-mana 5/5 flier ends games by itself in this format, and the ETB is close to free value in U/B where your graveyard already has a creature, an instant and a sorcery worth rebuying. Plan the mana around the double black.
Vigorbloom Charm: Flexible two-mana G/W playable that is never dead — protection against a removal spell, a cantrip with three life, or a pumped fight. Discount the fight mode as removal since it needs a body and loses to instant-speed answers, but the modality carries it.
Vigorbloom Vanguard // Seed Suture: Better than the grade. Two mana for a 2/2 plus a free counter and a life point is real value at uncommon, and the vigilance rider is a genuine attacking edge in a G/W deck already stacking counters. Nothing spectacular, but it's an early playable you're happy to have.
Vindictive Triumph: The best removal spell you'll see in W/B and a higher pick than 3.5 implies. Instant-speed unconditional exile with no drawback clears bombs and planeswalkers alike, and against cheap creatures you get a surprise attacker or blocker on top. Only the double black restricts it.
Warrior's Blades: High pick in R/W and the 3.0 grade is low. This is a 3-damage removal spell with three life stapled on that then sticks around as a repeatable +2/+1, and the equip cost drops toward free in the counters deck. Removal that keeps paying is the best kind here.
Whiplash Wordsmith // Vicious Verse: Better than the grade — the prepared spell self-enables the body. Cast the free Vicious Verse and the same turn you have a 3/3 flying haste for four, which is a real clock in B/R. Even blind it's a 3/3 that eventually connects for three in the air. Fine common.
Woodwork Prodigy // Soul Tether: High pick in R/G and one of the three prepared engines that actually re-arms. A three-mana 3/3 that mints a free Heartwood every upkeep ramps you, fixes you, and stacks artifact count for Craterclaw Colossus and Pia. Kill-on-sight for the opponent; grade it above 3.
Afterthought Sentry: Better than a 1.0. A colorless 2/2 for two goes in every deck without touching your mana, gains flying as a late-game mana sink, and incidentally strips U/B's threshold fuel on every attack. It's the 22nd or 23rd card, but it is a card.
Archive Arbiter: Playable colorless top-end, undergraded. Six mana for a 4/4 flier wins stalled boards in any deck regardless of colors, and it costs you nothing in deckbuilding. The destroy mode is often blank but occasionally answers an equipment or Pacifism effect; the four life is the real fallback. Mid-to-late pick that always makes decks.
Codie, Ravenous Codex: High ceiling, low floor — the copy trigger needs several prepared creatures and most decks field one or two, and the five-colour activation is decoration in Limited. What you're actually drafting is a colourless three-mana 1/4 that blocks the format's two-drops. Playable in any deck, exciting in almost none.
The Echoverse Fulcrum: Colorless catch-up mythic, playable in any deck but great in few. Two mana to loot is a fair early play; the seven-mana total to wrath means you want to be the deck that's behind. Terrible in R/W or W/U aggro, excellent in a grindy B/x pool.
Eye of Jace: Cut it. It affects nothing on board, the self-mill is too slow to reliably hit seven, and two damage plus two life is not worth a card. Even U/B threshold wants creatures that fill the yard while blocking. Sideboard at best.
Keeper of the Quiet Hour: Far better than the grade — a three-mana 3/2 that fits in literally every deck, makes a Jace token, and turns your common duals untapped from then on. It's not exciting, but it's a real playable in all ten pairs and the cheapest way to switch the land clause on.
Living Library: Better than it looks as a colourless defensive filler. An 0/4 for two blanks the aggressive two- and three-drops, it counts as an artifact for Pia and Craterclaw Colossus, and the eight-mana sacrifice is a real late-game answer to a bomb. Late pick, real playable.
Medic's Kitesail: Marginal playable that gets better the more your deck stalls. Fliers break board stalls here, and four total mana to hand one out is a fair price in a grindy G/W or W/x deck. Cut it from any deck with real evasion already; it's a fix for a problem, not a plan.
Murmuring Volume: Sideboard-ish filler. Fixing is already close to free here with ten common duals, so paying three mana for a rock that also loots at two mana a turn is a bad rate. Only playable when you're splashing two or three off-colour cards and need the extra land count.
Dedicated Commons: One of the ten common duals. Real in R/W because the planeswalker clause is live off any Jace token, but fixing is nearly free in this set and splashes are cheap, so this shouldn't beat a playable. Take it in the back half of a pack.
Deserted Beach: Low-priority even in W/U. The format hands out ten untapped-on-a-planeswalker duals at common and splashing is close to free, so a rare slot spent on fixing is a wasted pick. Play it if you're base W/U, but never take it over a creature or a removal spell.
Fatehold Annex: Low pick that fills a slot. The set already gives fixing away at common, so a dual is worth less here than the text suggests — its value is that it enters untapped once you have a Jace token, which W/U decks usually do. Take it last, play it, do not prioritise it.
Formidable Commons: Late pick, real inclusion. Fixing is close to free in this format with ten of these at common, so don't spend a pick above the last few on it. In B/G it's basically untapped — any Jace token from any empower card turns it on.
Hall of Echoes: Marginal — usually a sideboard land. A colorless source costs you real consistency even with the duals around, and five mana to copy a creature is a luxury sink most games never reach. Worth a slot only when your deck is nearly mono-colored and has a large creature worth doubling.
Haunted Ridge: Last-few-cards land. Fixing is already close to free here with ten common duals, so a rare that only fixes a pair you're already in adds little. Take it over nothing when you're B/R or splashing off black, never over a playable.
Hexhaven Dueling Arena: Skip it. Producing only colorless hurts a two-color mana base, and the re-prepare ability costs two to four mana in a deck that probably runs two prepared creatures. The three uncommon engines already re-prepare for free every upkeep. Sealed curiosity at best.
Innovative Commons: Take it middle-to-late, not early. Fixing is close to free in this set — ten of these at common — so it's worth less than the text implies, though the planeswalker clause makes it untapped often enough that U/R can run it without tempo loss.
Konstrari Annex: Take it late, play it in R/G, never take it over a playable. Fixing is close to free in this format with ten of these at common, and the untapped clause needs a Jace token you may not have. Also the cheapest way to support a single off-colour splash.
Meticulous Commons: Take it late. W/B is a top pair and the untapped condition is easy given how many cards make a Jace token, but fixing is nearly free in this format with ten of these at common — never pick it over a playable spell you would actually cast.
Overgrown Farmland: Worst kind of rare. Fixing is nearly free in this format — ten untapped-with-a-planeswalker duals at common — so a conditional G/W dual adds almost nothing. Play it if you're already G/W or splashing, never take it over a body or a removal spell.
Rockfall Vale: Free inclusion, never a pick. It's a worse version of the common R/G dual whenever you're empowering Jace, and about the same otherwise. Take it as a late wheel in R/G, but never over a spell — this format does not reward drafting fixing.
Roiling Canopy: Unplayable. Six other Forests in a two-colour deck is a fantasy, and you're paying a tapped land for the privilege of trying. The 0.0 is correct — this is a rare that never makes a Limited deck.
Room of Refuge: Sideboard fixing. Entering tapped costs a real turn in a format where the common duals often come in untapped, and the five-mana counter sink is a sad way to spend a land. Only for a genuine three-colour build that lacks the right dual.
Shipwreck Marsh: Filler despite the rare slot. Turn-one and turn-two it is a tapland, which is exactly when you wanted it untapped; after that it is a Swamp-Island. In a format with ten common duals and easy splashes, this is the least interesting rare you will open.
Stingerquill Annex: The most-played of the ten common duals, because B/R is the best pair — which also means it wheels less often than the others. Still a last-few-picks card. Any empower effect produces a Jace token and it enters untapped.
Theorist's Sanctum: Fine in heavy blue, overrated at this grade. It's an Island that sometimes enters tapped plus a late-game mana sink — real, but it competes with spells for a slot, and the empower activation is slow value, not a win condition. Take it in blue Jace decks; it's not a first pick.
Theorix Annex: Late wheel pick that does its job cheaply. It enters untapped the moment you have any Jace token, which U/B decks will, so it's a strictly-fine dual for the pair. With ten of these at common, fixing costs you almost nothing — never spend a real pick on it.
Transformative Commons: Late pick even in its colors. Fixing is nearly free here — ten of these at common — and this one serves G/U, the pair with the fewest removal spells in the set. Take it if you're already there, never as a reason to go there.
Vigorbloom Annex: Same read as the rest of the cycle: a fine 23rd card, never a pick over a playable. G/W's higher curve means the tapped turns hurt less, and one of these is enough to support a splashed removal spell or bomb.
Ajani Resolute: Trap mythic. Two mana for a walker whose only real ability is a 0 that gains one life means four idle turns before a 2/2 arrives, and creatures attack it down long before that. In G/W lifegain it ticks faster and could get there; everywhere else it's a do-nothing that also enables your duals.
Danitha, Sword of Hope: Conditional role-player. A 2/2 first strike for three is a below-rate body, so the draw trigger has to fire, which means a build with Equipment and combat tricks — R/W with Warrior's Blades. In a normal creature deck she is filler.
Ghalta the Immovable: Trap, and the grade is right. The discount needs a high-toughness creature already on board, so it's a five-or-six mana 0/7 that does nothing the turn it lands and needs friends with lopsided stats to matter. Build-around with no payoff density here.
Gideon's Memorial: Better than it looks, because the floor is high. You never have to cast it: from hand it's a two-mana instant-speed four damage to an attacker or blocker, which beats most white removal rates. The token anthem gives it a real ceiling in R/W Cadets; the planeswalker mana is dead text.
Koth of the Homestead: Modest role-player. A 2/3 for three blocks well and the Plains trigger accrues real counters in a heavy-white R/W counters deck, but the triggers are slow and the body doesn't threaten anything. Playable, never a priority pick.
Liliana the Faultless: Role-player with a specific job: a one-mana body that makes your bomb untargetable for {1} and a discard. That's insurance worth running in any deck with a must-answer threat, and the incidental lifegain feeds G/W Vigorbloom payoffs. The 1/1 body and card cost keep it below the grade.
Lyra, Archangel of Dawn: Early pick, near-bomb in the right shell. A three-mana 3/3 flier already beats most curves here, and the format's removal struggles with toughness 4 — which she reaches the first time you gain any life. In G/W lifegain she snowballs out of range by turn six.
Rescue Girl, First Responder: Marked up hard from 1.0. A three-mana 1/3 flier is a fine W/U body on its own, and the tap ability re-prepares your prepared creatures for a second free spell, rebuys ETBs like Fateshaper Aspirant, and rescues a permanent from sorcery-speed removal. Sorcery-speed-only is the limit.
Saheeli, Consul of Oversight: Near-bomb uncommon and a high pick in white. A 4/4 flier at five is already above rate for closing games, and this set is drowning in surveil — even the Jace token turns it on — so the Thopter stream is close to guaranteed every turn. W/U's best payoff for its own mechanic.
Teyo, Lightshield Expert: Solid W playable, mostly as a flash trick with a body attached. Held up, it blanks a removal spell and leaves a permanent +1/+1 counter, which is a clean two-for-one for two mana. The 1/1 is irrelevant; the value is in never tapping out.
Thalia, the Survivor: Graded low for what is a clean white playable. A 3/4 lifelink for four dodges the format's three-damage benchmark, blanks combat math, and swings races on its own. The tax is a rounding error in Limited, but you weren't paying for it anyway.
Tomik, Orzhov Lawmage: Good white two-drop. A 2/1 flier for two is already above rate in a format that breaks stalls on evasion, and giving flying to a counter-laden body makes R/W's go-wide draws lethal out of nowhere. Ignore the planeswalker text; it's a free rider.
Way of the Healer: Real engine and a high uncommon pick. Four mana buys a Jace at five loyalty that immediately makes a 2/2 Cadet with surveil and does it again next turn — repeatable bodies are exactly what breaks this format's stalls. Best in W/U surveil, fine in any white deck.
Way of the Mentor: Near-unplayable. Three mana for zero board presence in a format where games are decided by bodies and fliers, and the lifegain clause needs a dedicated shell to matter. The big empower number just means one extra Jace draw; sideboard.
Yoshimaru, Beloved Companion: Build-around role-player. Without a counters shell it's a three-mana 2/2 with a six-mana sink, which is unplayable; in R/W or G/W it makes every trick and Seed Suture a size bigger and stacks up quickly. Only take it after you've seen counter payoffs flowing.
Yuriko, Blade of the Mighty: Fringe playable, and the 2.0 is right. Locking combat shuts off the format's dense instant-speed removal while you attack, which is a genuine edge for an aggro deck, but it blanks your own tricks too and a 2/3 for four is well under rate. The double-strike clause fights any go-wide plan.
Arni, Humble Scribe: Better than a 2.5 in U/B. A 3/2 for three is already fine rate, the untap clause means you often loot on the same turn you deploy a creature, and repeatable filtering both fixes draws and fills the yard toward threshold. Solid mid-pick that grows in a grindy pool.
Chandra, Chill of Compliance: Bomb. A three-mana planeswalker that defends itself with stun counters and draws real cards off the first plus is close to unbeatable in a format this slow — every turn it survives is a card. Blue's biggest problem is that it can't kill things; this one can at least lock a threat down. First pick in blue.
Fblthp, Impossibly Lost: Underrated at 2.0 — this is a real card in W/U and R/W. Any attacker connecting, not just Fblthp, draws you two and shuffles him back to be drawn again. In an aggro deck with fliers or Cadets that is repeatable card advantage on a two-drop.
Geist of Saint Thalia: Solid two-drop with a real payoff attached. A 1/2 flier for two is already a W/U Fatehold playable; shaving a mana off every noncreature spell is the kind of discount U/R prowess and any removal-dense B/R deck converts into free turns. Take it over generic commons.
Hapatra, the Desert Frost: Solid blue playable and a strong tempo card. A 4/3 body at four is fine on its own; the stun counter is effectively two turns off their best blocker, which is as close to an answer as blue gets. Treat it as an attack-enabler for W/U aggro, not as removal.
Jace, Reality Sculptor: Good rare, not a bomb — it doesn't touch the board the turn it lands. The −3 fogs attacks for a full turn cycle so it protects itself, and the +1 builds a token that draws you cards. Wants a heavy-Islands blue deck; the ultimate is flavour text in Limited.
Lyra, Tolarian Archangel: First-pickable in blue, though I wouldn't quite give it a perfect grade. A three-mana 3/3 flier is already above rate in a format that stalls and breaks on evasion; the Angel clause needs three draws in a turn and will rarely fire. The five-mana sink is the real late game.
Proft, Consulting Detective: Strong uncommon and a repeatable mana sink, which is what long games in this set reward. Surveil is the most common keyword here and the Jace token surveils on its own, so Proft turns spare mana into cards and a growing clock. High pick in any blue deck.
Ruric Thar, Biomagus: Underrated at that grade — a 4/6 flier is a finisher and a wall at the same time, double prowess makes it a 6/8 on any cantrip, and the draw trigger means their removal spell isn't clean. Six mana is the only real knock. Near-bomb in U/R, playable in any blue deck.
Samut, Tyrant of Naktamun: A 2/1 for two with text that does almost nothing here — split second protects your spells from responses, and blue has no removal worth protecting. Play her as a warm body in a W/U tempo curve, and never pick her over a real card.
Tetsuko Umezawa, Fugitive: Below the grade — this is filler. A 1/3 blocks the format's two-drops and makes itself an unblockable one-power clock, which is not a plan, and blue's cheap fliers already have evasion so the text mostly reads blank. Sideboard material unless your pool is oddly full of small bodies.
Traxos, Academy Guardian: Underrated at 2.5 in the spell-dense decks. Cast it for two after any cheap noncreature spell and a 1/5 flier with vigilance blocks everything on the ground while prowess turns it into a clock. U/R and W/U want it highly; it's clunky and slow anywhere the discount rarely fires.
Way of the Cryomancer: Narrow engine, not a build-around to chase. Empower Jace 5 on turn three is a genuine draw engine and turns your duals untapped immediately, but it does nothing to the board and the copy ability wants a spell-dense deck. Mostly a G/U card — the trap pair. Leave it unless you're already there.
Way of the Mind Sculptor: Slow value, and the grade is too harsh. Five mana that affects nothing on board is bad, but a 5-loyalty Jace that draws two cards per activation is a genuine grind engine in a controlling blue deck. The problem is G/U is the trap pair and this needs the game to already be stable. Fringe playable.
Yargle, Goliath of Otaria: Filler that only a grindy blue deck wants. Nine toughness blanks the entire red removal suite and stops every ground attacker, but five mana that never closes a game is a poor deal in a format where stalls break on fliers and the Jace token. Sideboard against aggro.
Yuriko, Hope from the Shadows: Playable, not exciting. One mana flash means you ambush with a surveil 2 and a chump blocker for free, and the -X/-0 mode shuts down an attacker once your graveyard is stocked — but it never kills anything. Best in U/B, where the graveyard is already the plan.
Danitha, Spear of Agony: Good in B/R, filler outside it. First strike on a two-drop already trades up, and in the removal-densest pair in the format she grows most turns you interact — a 4/4 first striker by turn five is real pressure. In a low-interaction black deck she's just a 2/2.
Gallia, Tragic Host: Strong two-drop in the colour that has the fewest. Two-power menace pressures early, and once the game grinds she buys herself back with a counter, so she's live in both halves of the game. Good in W/B and B/R; take her over most black commons.
Garruk, Veiled Butcher: Bomb — take it over any removal spell. The static line exiles everything they lose, +2 kills small creatures while protecting loyalty, −2 is an edict that nets a 4/4 trampler, and it's a real planeswalker so your duals come in untapped. Win the game if unanswered.
Gideon the Oathless: Solid rare on stats alone. A 3/3 for three with ward is hard to answer cleanly, and the pings add up fast against the creature decks. It's a B/R reach card wearing a rare's clothing — excellent playable, not a game-winner you build around.
Liliana the Repentant: Good rare that starts as a two-drop and ends as a reanimation spell. The mill is genuine fuel for U/B threshold rather than a drawback, and the exhaust ability gives a cheap body late-game relevance. Black is short on two-drops, so this fills two slots at once.
Loot, the Anomaly: Sneaky-good three-drop. A 2/4 body blocks the format's ground creatures well, and the threshold ability reads backwards — each −2/−0 makes his combat damage bigger, so a late-game sacrifice turn hits hard. Wants U/B threshold or W/B attrition with fodder to spare.
Mabel, Bitter Recluse: Fine cheap playable in W/B and B/G. A one-mana deathtouch blocker holds off anything for the early turns and trades up all game, and the counter removal quietly blanks an opposing R/W or G/W counters threat or strips a Jace token. Low ceiling, high floor.
Massacre Girl, Most Wanted: Strong B/R uncommon that grows itself — her own drain trigger feeds her counters, so any board where creatures trade snowballs her out of removal range. Also excellent in W/B attrition. Docked only because a five-mana 4/4 with no evasion and no immediate impact can be answered clean.
Proft, Sinister Mastermind: Underrated at 2.0 because it is never a dead card. Early it cycles as a -3/-1 combat trick for one black; late, with seven in the yard, it's a 5/5 menace for three that ends games. That flexibility makes it a strong U/B and W/B pick.
Teyo, Diamondblade Mage: Underrated — it targets itself. Flash in a 4/2 deathtouch blocker and you eat their best creature for four mana at instant speed, which beats what most black commons offer. Flexible enough to protect a planeswalker or push a counter instead. Solid playable, well above the grade.
Tinybones, Pocket Nuisance: Role-player in B/R. Three mana for a 2/1 is bad rate, so you are paying for the ETB: one card stripped plus one to the face, with more damage if your deck has other discard. Fits the face-burn plan, filler anywhere else.
Way of the Deathbringer: Undergraded at 1.5. Turn three this is an instant 5-loyalty Jace with a repeatable -2 that converts spare bodies into 4/4 tramplers — a threat engine for W/B and B/G attrition decks that already want to trade creatures. Does nothing the turn it lands, so it is bad when you're behind.
Way of the Necromancer: Cut it in most decks. Two mana that affects nothing on board is a bad trade in a format where a Jace token only surveils and draws slowly, and you need heavy creature death before the loyalty accrual matters. Only worth a slot in a W/B attrition deck that also has Compel Brutality.
Winter, Tormented Loner: Role-player in W/B attrition and little else. The edict wants fodder you're happy to lose — a token or a dying creature — and the 0/3 only threatens once the graveyard fills, which takes real turns. Fine playable in the sacrifice deck, weak filler anywhere else.
Yargle, Glutton of Urborg: Nearly unplayable. Three damage kills most of this format's creatures, so a five-mana 9/3 dies to every common removal spell and chump-blocks into nothing. Only consider it in B/R with trample from Hunter's Axe or Ajani's Anguish, and even then it's your 23rd card.
Ajani Unrelenting: Bomb, first pick out of any pack. The −3 is a one-sided wrath that leaves your Cadets standing, and every activation adds another 2/2, so it protects itself while taking over. Six mana is the only real cost. Splash it if you have to.
Arni, Renowned Champion: Defensive filler. A four-mana 1/5 walls the format's common creatures well but attacks for nothing unless you're deploying a body every turn — that means R/W Cadets or nothing. Playable 22nd card in a go-wide deck, sideboard in anything with a real curve.
Chandra, Torch of Defiance: First pick out of any pack. Four mana, protects herself by killing most of the format with −3, and every other turn is either a free card or two damage to the face. Double red is the only cost, and this format's common duals make that easy to support.
Gallia, the Merrymaker: Good R/W two-drop. A 2/1 haste is on rate for aggro, and the repeatable counter-plus-haste sink converts flooded turns into pressure while feeding the pair's counter payoffs. Take it as a solid playable in red aggro; it's just a 2/1 anywhere else.
Jiang Yanggu, Alone: Playable body, ignore most of the text. A 4/4 menace for five gets through in stalls, which is the reason to play it; attacking alone to rummage for one counter is a trigger you'll rarely want and one that actively fights a wide board. Mid-pack R playable, slightly above 1.5.
Kiora of Fire and Ashes: Higher than a 3.0 — this is seven power across two bodies for six, and the 5/5 flier alone breaks the board stalls this format produces. The 2/2 shell dying to anything is fine because the Dragon is the card. Solid top-end for any red deck.
Koth, the Geomancer: Good three-drop, slightly underrated. A 3/2 with reach blocks the fliers that break this format's stalls, and the landfall ping is inevitable chip damage plus a genuine payoff enabler in B/R — it turns on noncombat-damage checks like Whiplash Wordsmith for free. Take it in any red deck.
Marwyn, the Clearcutter: Better than a 2.0 in R/G. A one-mana 2/1 is a fine aggro body on its own, and with Heartwood tokens the activation stops being a real cost — spent tokens turn into cards all game. Outside a deck making artifacts it is a one-drop that sacrifices lands; just filler.
Pia, Determined Rebuilder: Solid three-drop. Three power split across two bodies with a flier is fine on rate anywhere, and the Thopter plus Pia count toward R/G's artifact payoffs alongside Heartwoods. The pump costs six mana, so treat it as a mana sink in long games rather than a reason to play the card.
Samut, Hazoret's Champion: Solid aggro two-drop, not a rare-quality bomb. The 2/2 haste body is the bulk of the card and fits R/W and R/G curves; the team-wide haste is a small but real bonus when you're ramping into Heartwood-powered top-end. Play it in any aggressive red deck, don't pick it over removal.
Tetsuko Umezawa, Pursuer: Better than the 3.0 — a four-mana double striker that hits for four while surviving the format's 3-damage removal is a genuine problem to block. Prowess pushes it out of range entirely in U/R. Take it high in any red deck; it attacks and defends equally well.
Tomik, Izzet Sparkmage: Better than a 2.5 in the right pair. B/R Stingerquill is built on noncombat damage, and this quietly upgrades every burn spell — No Admittance becomes four, Vicious Verse becomes two to the face. Prowess two-drop body means it's never dead. Mediocre outside B/R and U/R.
Way of the Pyromancer: Overrated at 2.5. Two mana for no board presence is a real cost in a format where three damage kills most creatures, and turning Jace into a ritual only pays in a deck already stuffed with empower cards. Niche G/U or Jace-dedicated pick.
Way of the Warlord: Good in B/R face-burn, mediocre elsewhere. Three mana to Shock a creature and hit the opponent for two is a fair rate, and if your deck has other empower cards feeding the same token it becomes repeatable reach, which is how that pair wins. One copy of empower isn't enough.
Winter, Team Player: Role-player for go-wide decks. Five mana for a 3/3 is unplayable at face value; convoke routinely makes him a two- or three-mana play in R/W Cadets, where the anthem trigger turns a stalled board into lethal. In a low-count creature deck, leave him out.
Edgar, Moonlit Sovereign: Solid uncommon with a real floor. A five-mana 4/4 with flash already wins combat outright, and if you have a turn where you do nothing else it snowballs into something that needs two removal spells. The 'didn't cast a spell' clause is awkward, so value it as a good body with upside, not an engine.
Fblthp, Knows the Way: Trap at 3.0. In a normal two-colour deck this is a */2 that pays X to draw you lands you didn't need — fixing is already free here with ten common duals, and the power ceiling wants a greedy four-colour mana base that's worse than just playing a clean deck. Weak body, expensive.
Garruk, Curse Breaker: Bomb, first pick out of any pack. Minus three immediately makes a 4/4 trampler that outclasses the format's commons and protects him, the ultimate ends a stalled board, and the draw trigger turns on off his own token. Splash him if you have to.
Ghalta the Unstoppable: High ceiling, brick floor. Realistically this costs six or seven in R/G after Heartwood ramp and a fat body, and when it lands the trample anthem ends the game immediately. But draw it before you have a big creature and it's a dead card for four turns. Late playable in R/G only.
Jiang Yanggu, Never Alone: Solid playable everywhere in green. Four mana for five stats across two bodies plays well on both sides of the board, and the untap clause quietly means Heartwood tokens make mana on your turn and still untap for theirs. Above-average, not a card to build around.
Loot, the Nexus: Marked down from 3.0. It's a 2/1 for three that dies to everything and only ramps once you already have a diverse board — by which point you want threats, not mana, and this format's ten common duals have already solved your fixing. Modest R/G ramp filler.
Marwyn, the Preserver: The body is the whole card, and it's a fine one. A 3/2 for two attacks past most early blockers, but the hexproof and land recursion are effectively blank in Limited. Green is deep in two-drops, so this is a good-not-great playable rather than a priority pick.
Pia, Aether Ascetic: Filler. The tutor is only live if you drafted an enchantment worth finding, and most pools have zero to two, so this is usually a three-mana 2/2 with a discard outlet stapled on. Playable if green is short; nothing to prioritize.
Ruric Thar, Magecrusher: Legitimate top end, not an expensive vanilla. Hexproof until it connects means removal can't answer it before it swings, and reach plus vigilance plus trample covers both sides of a stall. Seven mana is the cost; R/G Heartwood ramp is how you pay it. One per deck.
Titanbones, Towering Heart: Solid four-drop, excellent in G/W. Reach on a 4/3 already blocks the fliers that break stalls, and a single lifegain trigger makes it a 6/5 that dominates combat. The discard clause is a small bonus with the set's landcyclers.
Way of the Paradox: Skip it. Three mana that affects nothing on board, and the ramp only triggers when you activate loyalty — so you need another empower card, a spare land in hand, and time. This is the G/U trap card in miniature: cute engine, no board impact, weakest pair in the set.
Way of the Wildspeaker: Slow but real top-end. Five mana does nothing the turn it lands, then makes a 4/4 trample each turn for two turns off the Jace token, which breaks the board stalls this format produces. Only G/U and green ramp decks want it; do not pick it early.
Yoshimaru, Scrappy Stray: Green's removal is fight effects and this is one of the better ones, but discount it: you need a bigger body already down, and it's two-for-one'd by instant-speed removal in response. Still a high pick in a green deck because the colour has so few answers — just don't run it out on turn two.
Edgar, Ancient Bloodlord: High pick for W/B. Black is the shallowest colour at two-drops and a 2/3 body blocks the format's early creatures well, so the rate alone is fine; the sac outlet then converts spare tokens and dying creatures into a menace threat that ends long games. Premium in Liliana's Attrition.
Hapatra, the Desert Fang: Strong uncommon with a variance tail. By turn five your yard usually holds a four-or-five-drop, so this is a 3/3 plus a hard kill on their best creature — but it can whiff into a nearly empty graveyard on an early curve-out. B/G pays it off best.
Karn, Gilded Guardian: Trap. In a two-colour deck you're paying eight mana for a 5/5 with vigilance and trample and an ETB that draws roughly zero, because you won't control multicoloured artifacts. The hybrid cost looks flexible and isn't. Leave it in the sideboard unless you're a genuine artifact deck.
Kiora of Salt and Sand: Fine body, small upside, G/U only. A three-mana 2/4 blocks the format's aggressive two-drops well, and a Jace token's -1 turns on the unblockable trigger every turn if you want it. The -8 Leviathan grant is decoration. Playable if you are in the pair, not a reason to be.
Mabel, Valley Hero: Higher than 2.0 in R/W Ajani's Army. It counters itself up on entry and then every creature you play afterward arrives a size bigger, which is exactly the go-wide-plus-counters plan. A 1/2 for three is a lightning rod, so it needs to survive a turn to pay off. Near-blank outside R/W.
Saheeli, Jewel of Avishkar: High pick in U/R, near-unplayable elsewhere. The 2/4 body holds the ground while every noncreature spell adds a hasty flier — and fliers are how this format's stalls break. In a prowess deck with double-digit spells it takes over games; in anything else it's a four-mana wall.
Tam, the Possibility: Near-blank text on a fine body. Real planeswalkers barely exist in packs so the cost reduction almost never triggers, and the WUBRG ability is uncastable. What's left is a three-mana 2/4 blocker in G/U, the pair with the least removal. Filler at best.
Vraska, Soul of Stone: Powerful and hard to cast. Three colors with no allied pair behind it means you need the duals to line up, and the token engine only hums in a spells-heavy U/R deck splashing white. Mark it down a notch for castability; it's a build-around, not a slam.
Vraska, the Cutting Glare: Premium B/G rare — evaluate it as a three-mana 4/4 deathtouch and take it early. Nothing in the format blocks it profitably and it stonewalls the ramp decks' top end. The destroy trigger almost never turns on when you cast it on curve; treat it as pure upside on a late draw.
Karn, Argent Defender: Sideboard only, and even there be careful — the effect is symmetric and this set is dense with ETB creatures, Cadet makers and empower triggers on your own side. Two mana for a colourless 1/3 blocker that fits any deck; bring it in against a deck built entirely on entry triggers.
Traxos, Scourge Eternal: Above its grade and colourless, so every deck can play it. A 5/4 trample for four outclasses the format's common creatures, and any creature-dense deck casting a spell most turns keeps him untapping. Discount him only if your curve is light on creatures and artifacts.
Emrakul, the Exigent Doom: Unplayable in draft. Ten mana is out of reach even for R/G Heartwood ramp, and the exile-for-mana mode turns it into an overpriced Rampant Growth rather than a threat. Sideboard it; the only realistic home is a Sealed pool with heavy acceleration and nothing else to do.
Return to the Light Realms: Unplayable. Nine mana for a sorcery that does nothing to the board unless your graveyard is already stacked, in a format where games end before that. Zero is the correct grade.
Seasoned Cryomancer: High pick, though a touch below a 4.0 — it doesn't dominate a board on its own. Filtering four cards deep while stunning two blockers is a real tempo turn for a three-drop, and the graveyard activation means it's still a card in the long games this format produces.
Darklight Phoenix: Strong playable, short of a true bomb. A four-mana 3/2 flying haste is a fine rate on its own, and the recursion is live most turns in W/B attrition or B/R where creatures trade constantly. In a durdly green deck it stays dead in the yard, so value it by your deck's trade rate.
Omnipresence: Trap, cut it. Eight mana for an enchantment that affects nothing on resolution, in a format where 68% of spells cost three or less — so even a good board only frees up the cards you could already cast. You lose the game on the turn you tap out for it.
